title: "I Was Exposed 24x7": Why Virat Kohli Walked Away From Captaincy
excerpt: In a candid podcast appearance, India's greatest modern batter reveals the toll of leading in the spotlight—and why stepping down was the best decision he ever made
body:
"I Was Exposed 24x7": in a rare and deeply candid appearance on RCB's Bold Diaries podcast, Virat Kohli has laid bare the mental and emotional toll of leading India and Royal Challengers Bengaluru for the better part of a decade. His revelations—about faking intensity, the unbearable weight of constant scrutiny, and ultimately choosing personal happiness over public expectation—offer the most complete account yet of why one of cricket's fiercest competitors walked away from leadership.

## The burden of wearing two crowns

For seven years in international cricket and nine at the helm of RCB, Kohli shouldered a double captaincy that few modern cricketers have attempted. "In every game, there were expectations from me as a batter," he said, describing a relentless cycle where every dismissal invited questions about his captaincy and every tactical misstep triggered a post-mortem of his batting. "I was exposed to it 24x7, and it got too much in the end."

The timeline tells its own story. Kohli first relinquished the India T20I captaincy after the 2021 World Cup, before stepping away from RCB's leadership at the close of that IPL season. By January 2022, following a bruising Test series loss to South Africa, he resigned as Test captain too—bringing the curtain down on a tenure that included 40 Test victories, the most by any Indian skipper.

## When intensity became performance

Perhaps the most striking admission came when Kohli described a period in which his famous competitive fire had become an act. "I realised I was trying to kind of fake my intensity a bit," he confessed. The revelation led to a month-long break from cricket in 2022—a spell in which he did not pick up a bat. "I reached a point where I wasn't happy in the spotlight," he said. "If I have decided I want to be in this place, I need to be happy."

That sabbatical marked a turning point. Kohli returned to international cricket ahead of the 2022 Asia Cup reinvigorated, and went on to play a pivotal role in India's T20 World Cup campaign. He has spoken openly about depression and mental health struggles dating back to a difficult 2014 tour of England, and has since become one of cricket's most prominent advocates for players taking time away from the game when they need it.

## Gratitude for the early mentors

Even while recounting the hardships, Kohli reserved warm words for those who shaped his career before captaincy consumed it. MS Dhoni and coach Gary Kirsten, he said, entrusted a raw, self-doubting young batter with the number three position. "I was very realistic about my game. I didn't feel I was close to others in terms of skill. The only thing I had was determination," he reflected—a striking piece of humility from a man who went on to amass more than 27,000 international runs across formats, 85 international centuries, and over 8,500 runs for RCB alone.

## A story that resonates far from home

For the millions of NRI cricket fans who set alarms for inconvenient time zones and cluster around screens in living rooms from New Jersey to Melbourne, Kohli's captaincy era was not merely sport—it was identity. He captained during the explosive growth of cricket streaming abroad, the era when Willow TV and Hotstar transformed diaspora viewing from grainy illegal streams to polished subscription services. His image adorned shop windows in Southall and Jackson Heights alike.

His candid discussion of mental health carries particular weight in diaspora communities, where the pressure to perform and maintain appearances can mirror the very scrutiny Kohli describes. For second-generation South Asians raised on the mythology of "fight through everything," hearing their sporting hero say "I need to be happy" is quietly revolutionary.

Former India coach Ravi Shastri, who worked closely with Kohli through much of his captaincy tenure, recently echoed these sentiments, noting that the mental burnout from constant leadership demands was real and under-acknowledged. The message is clear: even the most driven competitors have limits, and recognising them is strength, not weakness.

## What comes next

Having shed the armband, Kohli has enjoyed what he describes as a "happy space"—free to focus on his batting without the weight of tactical decisions and selection controversies. With the 2026 IPL season in its closing stages and RCB sitting atop the standings at 18 points, the 37-year-old's decision to step back from leadership looks, in hindsight, like one of the shrewdest calls of his career. The franchise he could never lead to a title as captain won their maiden crown last year, with Kohli contributing as a liberated senior batter rather than an overburdened skipper.

For Kohli, the message is simple: sometimes the bravest thing a leader can do is stop leading. And for the millions who follow his every move from across oceans, that lesson extends well beyond the cricket pitch.
